title: How do you use Porter's five forces to judge an industry in a case?
description: Five forces (Porter) for case interviews. How attractive is this industry? Useful inside market entry and acquisitions.
hook: Use Porter's five forces to judge how hard it is to make money in an industry: look at rivalry, the threat of new entrants, substitutes, buyer power and supplier power, then name the strongest force and what it does to prices and margins. It tells you about the industry, not whether a particular company or deal is good.
body:
When it helps

Michael Porter set out the five forces in Harvard Business Review in 1979. In a case, use them to answer "How attractive is this industry?" That question sits inside market entry, acquisition and private equity cases, usually as one branch of the structure rather than the whole of it.

The checklist

Rivalry

  • Number and size of competitors
  • Price wars, slow growth, high fixed costs

New entrants

  • Barriers to entry: capital, licences, brand, scale

Substitutes

  • Other ways to meet the same need

Buyer power

  • A few big customers?
  • Low switching costs

Supplier power

  • A few suppliers?
  • Unique inputs

An example: a chain of independent gyms

Should a client buy a chain of independent gyms? Rivalry: many gyms, and budget chains compete hard on price. New entrants: a new gym needs a lease and equipment, so barriers are fairly low. Substitutes: running, home workouts, fitness apps. Buyer power: members can leave easily, though each one is small. Supplier power: equipment makers and landlords have some leverage, but not much.

Together that says gyms are a hard industry in which to earn high margins, so the target needs a clear edge. The next questions are about the company, not the industry: site-level occupancy, rent, member retention and what makes these gyms different locally. A tough industry can still contain a very good operator.

Make every force specific

A force is only useful if you say what it does to profit. Compare:

Weak: "Buyer power is high."
Strong: "Two customers account for 70% of revenue and can demand price cuts every year, so margins will stay under pressure."

The second version is a hypothesis you can test with data, and it changes what the client should pay.

How it sounds in an interview

"Before looking at the company itself, I'd check how attractive the industry is: rivalry, how easy it is to enter, substitutes, and the power of customers and suppliers. Then I'll say which force matters most for margins."

Common mistakes

  • Walking through all five forces at equal length. Spend your time on the one or two that matter.
  • Treating it as a scoring sheet that makes the decision. A good industry does not justify any price, and a tough one can still hold a good company.
  • Forgetting the company. Five forces is about the industry; you still need to test the client or target.

Practise it

1. Which force is usually strongest for a company that makes car parts for a handful of large carmakers?

Show the answer

Buyer power. A few very large customers buy most of the output, can switch suppliers between model generations and can push for annual price cuts. Ask what share of revenue the top three customers account for.

2. Give a two-sentence five forces view of a city's taxi industry after ride-hailing apps arrived.

Show the answer

Ride-hailing apps lowered the barriers to entry, because any driver with a car can join, and they gave riders more choice, so rivalry and buyer power both rose. The likely result is pressure on fares and drivers' earnings, so the questions are which players have scale or loyalty and whether regulation limits supply.
